explanations.explanation: That's the line, friend. The LORD says to David's Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.” (Psalm 110:1) Notice He says sit. Nobody has to scramble, because the LORD says He will handle the footstool part.

Guard duty would make sense if you picture a bakery night shift, and I've pulled a few. But nothing in the psalm puts David's Lord at a gate. The LORD says, “Sit at My right hand…” (Psalm 110:1). This is a seat of honor, not a post to watch.

explanations.answer: Go out ahead of My army
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think so, since the psalm has battle in it later. But the first command is a quiet one. The LORD says, “Sit at My right hand…” (Psalm 110:1). Sitting, friend, not marching out front.

Yes! The LORD says, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.” (Psalm 110:1) Look at who is doing the work there. The LORD says “I make.” So David's Lord gets to sit while the LORD takes care of it.

Careful, friend, this one is true. The LORD says, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.” (Psalm 110:1) The words are “I make,” and the LORD is the One speaking. David's Lord sits while the LORD does the making.

explanations.answer: Rule in the midst of Your enemies
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD extends the scepter from Zion and says, “Rule in the midst of Your enemies.” (Psalm 110:2) A scepter is what a ruler holds, so the words fit it. And the rule happens right in the middle of those enemies, which is a bold place to set up shop.

explanations.answer: Make peace with all Your enemies
explanations.explanation: Nice thought, friend, and I love a peacemaker. But that's not what the LORD says here. He says, “Rule in the midst of Your enemies.” (Psalm 110:2). The scepter is a ruler's tool, and the command is to rule.

explanations.answer: Go back and wait in Your tent
explanations.explanation: No tent in this psalm, friend. The LORD extends the scepter from Zion and says, “Rule in the midst of Your enemies.” (Psalm 110:2) That's a command to rule, and a tent is nowhere in the picture.
Not quite, friend. David says, “Your people shall be willing on Your day of battle.” (Psalm 110:3) Willing means they step up on their own. Nobody is hauling anybody by the ankles.

Right, and that's the whole point of the line. David says, “Your people shall be willing on Your day of battle.” (Psalm 110:3) Willing means no dragging, no begging, no bribing with a plate of cookies. Though I will say a plate of cookies never hurt anybody's attendance.

I see why you'd think so, since people leave themselves an out all the time. But the psalm says, “The LORD has sworn and will not change His mind…” (Psalm 110:4). Not change His mind. That means no escape hatch.

Yes! The psalm says, “The LORD has sworn and will not change His mind…” (Psalm 110:4). I once promised myself I'd only eat one broken cookie per batch. The LORD's oath is a different kind of promise, friend, because He will not change His mind.
Priest it is. The LORD swears, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” (Psalm 110:4) And look at that word forever. That's a long time to hold one job, friend.
Close, since prophets get a lot of attention in the Bible. But the LORD swears, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” (Psalm 110:4). The word is priest, and it comes with forever.
Shepherd is a lovely word, and David knew sheep up close. But in this verse the LORD swears, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” (Psalm 110:4). The word He swears is priest.

That's the word, friend. David says, “The Lord is at Your right hand; He will crush kings in the day of His wrath.” (Psalm 110:5) It's a heavy verse, and I think it's okay to let it be heavy. The word to hold on to is kings.

Giants make a good story, and David knew about one. But here David says, “He will crush kings in the day of His wrath.” (Psalm 110:5). The psalm names kings, and giants aren't in it. It's a heavy verse, friend.
Shepherds are fine, friend, and David was one himself. But this verse says, “He will crush kings in the day of His wrath.” (Psalm 110:5). The psalm names kings, and shepherds don't show up here.

That's right. David says of Him, “He will judge the nations, heaping up the dead…” (Psalm 110:6). It's the same One from verse 5 who crushes kings, and now He judges the nations. This part of the psalm is heavy, friend, so I'll let it stay heavy.

This one's true, friend. Verse 5 says He will crush kings in the day of His wrath, and verse 6 goes on with “He will judge the nations, heaping up the dead…” (Psalm 110:6). It's one picture with one Person doing it. It's a heavy stretch of the psalm, and I think it's okay to feel that.

That's how the psalm ends. “He will drink from the brook by the road; therefore He will lift up His head.” (Psalm 110:7) See that word therefore? The head lifting comes because of the drink. That's a quiet ending after a loud psalm, friend.

A rest after all that sounds nice, and I'd sign up. But the psalm doesn't say that. It says, “He will drink from the brook by the road; therefore He will lift up His head.” (Psalm 110:7). The last move is a lifted head.

Home is a good place, friend, but the psalm never sends Him there. It ends, “He will drink from the brook by the road; therefore He will lift up His head.” (Psalm 110:7). The drink comes first, then the head goes up.
